headline: OKC's look is red dirt, Route 66 neon, Deco-meets-Plains geometry and a Native design lineage that is the state's real visual ground, with the Thunder's sunset palette as the city's shared flag.
summary: Oklahoma City's visual culture is built by small, fiercely local districts (the Plaza, Paseo, Automobile Alley, Deep Deuce) rather than one famous mural wall, and it sits inside a state where 39 tribal nations are the deepest design heritage. The street language is mid-century roadside: Route 66 neon, hand-painted brick signs, Art Deco and Streamline Moderne. The color story is red clay and open prairie sky, and the Thunder's blue, sunset orange and yellow already read as the civic palette. For Nike, the opportunity is a City Edition and apparel story told through local makers (Native and Black Oklahoma artists first), not through Land Run or Western cliches.

insights.title: The districts are the scene
insights.detail: The Plaza District (NW 16th, anchored by the Plaza District Association and its mural program and festivals), the Paseo Arts District (Spanish Pueblo Revival bungalows, working studios) and Automobile Alley each have a distinct visual personality. Locals identify with a district more than with a citywide art brand.
insights.implication: Brief a district-by-district capsule or a collab series (Plaza, Paseo, Deep Deuce) instead of one generic OKC graphic; district names work as small-run graphic titles.

insights.title: Red dirt is the base color, sky blue is the field
insights.detail: Oklahoma clay reads as a deep oxide red and the state flag's field is a flat sky blue; together with the Thunder's blue and sunset orange, they sit very close to the team's own palette. Red dirt also names a whole local music and apparel idiom.
insights.implication: A red-clay colorway (washed, garment-dyed look) next to Thunder blue gives a premium alternative to the default blue-and-orange without leaving local truth.

insights.title: Roadside Route 66 and Deco lettering is the typographic vernacular
insights.detail: The city's signage memory is neon on Route 66 (Pops on the Arcadia stretch with its giant soda-bottle sign, motel and diner script), Automobile Alley showroom lettering, and Art Deco stepped forms in downtown and in Tulsa (Boston Avenue Methodist Church, Philtower). Hand-painted ghost signs and brick wall lettering are common in Bricktown and the Plaza.
insights.implication: Use script-and-block neon lettering, outlined slab type and stepped Deco geometry for graphics and jersey-number treatments; tie to a Route 66 centennial-era (2026) story only with licensing checked.

insights.title: Native design is the state's strongest authentic source and the highest-risk one
insights.detail: Oklahoma is home to Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee, Osage, Kiowa, Comanche and many other nations, with living artists such as Yatika Starr Fields (Cherokee/Osage/Muscogee, muralist and painter based in Tulsa). The Red Earth Festival in Oklahoma City is a long-standing venue for Native artists, and the state flag itself is built on an Osage battle shield.
insights.implication: Engage through a paid, credited collaboration with a Native artist or nation-approved partner; do not lift regalia, ceremonial patterns or tribal symbols as decoration, and keep Native work out of a team-branded graphic without that partnership.

insights.title: Deep Deuce and Northeast OKC carry the Black design story
insights.detail: Deep Deuce (Deep Second) was the Black jazz and business district that shaped Charlie Christian and Ralph Ellison; Northeast OKC and Tulsa's Greenwood district carry mural and memorial work around Black Wall Street. These stories are tied to real loss and recovery, and local Black artists, not outside brands, own the narrative.
insights.implication: If used, start with community partners and Black Oklahoma artists as lead creators with revenue share; Greenwood and the 1921 massacre are not a decorative theme.

insights.title: Thunder iconography is already the shared civic art
insights.detail: Thunder blue, sunset orange and yellow, the thunderbolt-and-basketball marks and the Loud City crowd culture are painted on walls, murals and shop fronts across the metro. Thunder fan art and local print makers sell heavily through gig posters, Plaza shops and fan markets.
insights.implication: Local artist collabs on official product should be framed as a flip on Thunder colors, not a competing identity; allow artists to reinterpret the team's sunset and storm sky.

places.name: Plaza District
places.why: The city's densest cluster of murals, indie shops, studios and gig-poster culture, and home of a long-running mural and festival program.

places.name: Paseo Arts District
places.why: Spanish Pueblo Revival studios and galleries with working artists, and host of the Paseo Arts Festival.

places.name: Oklahoma Contemporary Arts Center
places.why: The state's leading contemporary art venue, with studios, exhibitions and a purpose-built campus that anchors Midtown design culture.

places.name: Oklahoma City Museum of Art
places.why: Houses a major Chihuly glass collection and the 50-plus-foot Chihuly tower that is a recognizable city image.

places.name: Factory Obscura
places.why: Locally founded immersive and interactive art collective whose work has toured nationally; a credible collaborator for experiential activations.

places.name: Automobile Alley
places.why: Former auto showrooms with period lettering and murals, now a design and retail corridor.

places.name: Deep Deuce
places.why: Historic Black jazz district with markers and murals recalling Charlie Christian and Ralph Ellison.

places.name: Pops 66
places.why: A huge neon soda-bottle sign and glass-bottle wall make it the most photographed piece of Oklahoma roadside graphic design.

places.name: Tulsa Art Deco district and Philbrook Museum
places.why: Tulsa holds the state's richest Art Deco stock and a deep arts bench including the Tulsa Artist Fellowship.

places.name: Red Earth Festival
places.why: Annual juried showcase for Native American artists and dancers that is a respected entry point into Native art networks.

people.name: Yatika Starr Fields
people.why: Internationally exhibited Oklahoma muralist whose bold, color-saturated large walls make him a credible Native collaborator if engaged on his terms.

people.name: Factory Obscura
people.why: Homegrown OKC team behind interactive installations; fits experiential or store-environment work.

people.name: Oklahoma Contemporary Arts Center
people.why: A natural partner for artist-in-residence or studio collaboration programs with local makers.

people.name: Plaza District Association
people.why: Organizes mural commissions and festivals; the right first call for walls and pop-ups in the Plaza.

people.name: Paseo Arts Association
people.why: Runs the Paseo Arts Festival and represents resident studio artists.

people.name: Tulsa Artist Fellowship
people.why: Brings and retains working artists in Tulsa; a pipeline for credible state-level collaborators.

people.name: Charlie Christian and Ralph Ellison (honored legacies)
people.why: Their legacy is a reference for district storytelling; any use requires estate and community conversation, not a graphic lift.

moments.name: Festival of the Arts
moments.why: Long-running downtown outdoor art festival that draws the broadest local audience; timing overlaps the NBA playoffs.

moments.name: Paseo Arts Festival
moments.why: Neighborhood-scale juried art fair in the Paseo; Thunder playoff run often overlaps.

moments.name: Red Earth Festival
moments.why: Major Native arts and dance gathering in Oklahoma City.

moments.name: Oklahoma State Fair
moments.why: Peak display of Oklahoma vernacular graphics: midway lettering, livestock and craft ribbons.

moments.name: Plaza District Festival and mural events
moments.why: Neighborhood block party with live painting and local makers, close to preseason.

moments.name: Opening night and NBA Cup nights
moments.timing: Oct 20 start, Cup group play Fridays from Oct 30
moments.why: The Thunder's season opens at San Antonio and home Cup Fridays give early windows for district pop-ups and mural reveals.

moments.name: Juneteenth in Northeast OKC and Greenwood (Tulsa)
moments.why: The most important annual moment for Black Oklahoma art and memory, led by local organizations.

vocabulary.meaning: The Thunder fan identity at Paycom Center, tied to the crowd's volume.
The team's rallying call and fan phrase.
Oklahoma's clay soil, also shorthand for a local music and lifestyle idiom.
How locals refer to the two arts districts without the word 'district'.
Local name for the historic Black district along Second Street east of downtown.
The canal-side entertainment district of converted brick warehouses; locals rarely call it art.
A self-applied identity with pride in locals, with a Dust Bowl history that outsiders should not use as a joke.
The Thunder's bison mascot, a local favorite for kids and fan art.

designCues.cue: Thunder sunset orange against prairie sky blue
designCues.source: Thunder sunset orange, which also echoes Oklahoma sunsets and Route 66 neon
designCues.use: Lead accent on a City Edition or lifestyle capsule; pair with Thunder blue for a coherent local palette.

designCues.cue: Thunder blue as the sky field
designCues.source: Thunder primary color and the sky-blue state flag field
designCues.use: Base color for tees, warm-ups and shorts.
Garment-dyed or washed fleece and tees with an earthy finish; a tone-on-tone dirt-splatter print.

designCues.cue: Neon script and outlined slab lettering
designCues.source: Route 66 motel, diner and soda signs; Automobile Alley showroom lettering
designCues.use: Wordmark lockups and number treatments with a glow outline, rendered in reflective or glow-in-the-dark ink.

designCues.source: Downtown OKC and Tulsa Deco architecture
designCues.use: Tonal jacquard or embossed trim on jackets and jersey side panels.

designCues.source: Storm-front skies, tornado-season horizons and the Thunder name
designCues.use: Gradient fades on shorts and hoodies; avoid literal tornado or disaster imagery.

designCues.source: Ghost signs on Bricktown, Plaza and Automobile Alley walls
designCues.use: Distressed print finish on retro graphic tees; keep legible.

productHooks: A district capsule series (Plaza, Paseo, Deep Deuce) with one local artist per release, credited on the hangtag and paid royalties.
A Route 66 neon-script warm-up or fleece, built on Thunder sunset orange and dark navy, timed to the Route 66 centennial year.
A red-clay garment-dyed hoodie and tee set with a restrained Thunder-blue mark for fan and lifestyle retail.
A Native artist co-created collection, led by a Native designer with full credit and payment, released with a community event rather than a drop alone.
Court-side or store-environment art installations commissioned from Factory Obscura or Plaza District artists for launch events.
watchouts: Do not use tribal symbols, regalia, war bonnets or the Osage shield as decoration; engage Native artists directly and pay them.
The Land Run, Dust Bowl and cowboy imagery read as cliche and, for the Land Run, as dispossession; avoid or approach with Native input.
The Oklahoma City National Memorial and Tulsa's 1921 massacre are memorials, not graphic themes.
Route 66 signage, Pops and similar landmarks may carry trademark or sign-owner rights; license before reproducing.
The Plaza and Paseo associations and individual muralists own their murals; photos of walls on product need artist permission.
